items.title: Steve Wilson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 25, 2002
items.q: you had guys like Kenny Barron and Larry

ctx.x: We had mentioned the IAJE thing and it seems like it’s almost a necessity these days for jazz musicians to get involved in the education scene.

Yeah. Yeah I think fortunately, now I’ve seen the trend in the last ten years where more of the street musicians have gotten involved, musicians that are in the scene, of the scene, in addition to educators. And I think that’s been a positive. I think Bunky Green had a lot to do with that when he was president, to get a lot of the musicians involved. Of course I know that even before that there was — you had guys like Kenny Barron and Larry

Ridley who were teaching at Rutgers and then you had Rufus Reid who was head of the program at William Paterson for many years and recently retired. So there has always been that factor involved. But in the more recent times we’ve seen a big influx of that. And I hope that turns out to be a positive. Because again, education is good. But without the oral tradition, to get the unteachable nuances so to speak of the music, the spiritual elements of the music, there’s nothing like the oral tradition. There’s nothing…

items.title: Kenny Barron — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Then, the thing with Steve – Steve Wilson played on a few tracks. He was an amazing saxophonist. And Lionel also.

ctx.x: come out with this recording that very, very unique, with a lot of vocalists. Grady Tate’s on it. If you could talk a little bit more about that project.

Yeah. One of the things I wanted to do, there’s a friend of mine who lives in Tucson, Janice Jarrett, who’s written lyrics for, oh goodness, maybe 40 or 50 of my compositions. I thought, why don’t I record some of them, with the lyrics? So I chose three singers that I liked: Grechen Parlato, who I love; Ann Hampton Calloway, who a lot of people aren’t aware of. She’s – I made three or four recordings – three recordings with her. She’s a great, great singer, great intonation and great phrasing. And Grady Tate.…

Ken handed me a list of some unissued recordings and radio broadcasts. Some of these – many of these I’m not familiar with. So I’m just going to hand you the list and see if there’s anything – it starts here – if there’s anything there that you feel should be discussed for the historical record, since they’ll probably be ultimately released anyway. They’ll probably get into the public, given current technology, maybe because of licensing, maybe not as soon as I expect.
